item.title: Reconceptualizing Careers in Disruptive Times
item.content:encoded:
Jos Akkermans, VU University

David G. Collings, Trinity College Dublin

Mila Lazarova, Simon Fraser University

Jennifer Tosti-Kharas, Babson College

Career theory has evolved over recent decades. Classic career theories were grounded in relatively stable organizational contexts with hierarchical career paths and a relatively stable external context. In the 1990s, there was increasing recognition of the emergence of more flexible, dynamic careers, driven by technological disruption, demographic shifts, and the rise of non-traditional work and career paths. This development is still often referred to as the 'new career' paradigm. Career theories (e.g., boundaryless career theory, protean career theory, and social cognitive career theory) and concepts (e.g., career orientations, career competencies, and career self-management) within that paradigm primarily emphasize theorizing how individuals can take charge and successfully navigate volatile career paths.

However, the extent and pace of recent disruptions – including de-globalization, digitalization, platform-based work, climate challenges, and geopolitical instability – further challenge the core theoretical and conceptual foundations of what careers are and how they evolve over time. This context reinforces the need for novel theoretical perspectives on careers that move beyond individualized, linear models of careers toward more unpredictable, uncertain, dynamic, relational, and contextually embedded understandings of career development. In other words, we need a new 'new career' paradigm.

In many ways, the current context represents an inflection point for careers theory as several taken-for-granted assumptions are challenged and the boundary conditions of key theories are open to question. For example, the dominant agentic assumptions in research on core career-related constructs, such as employability, career success, calling, and career transitions, must be reconsidered to account for the fundamental shifts in how careers evolve today. Moreover, ongoing developments regarding (de-)globalization provide unique opportunities and threats to how careers take shape, and how such processes may differ across countries and cultures.

As another example of such fundamental shifts, the rise of non-traditional work arrangements and career paths renders core assumptions about careers, at least partially, invalid. For instance, gig work constitutes a series of micro-projects for multiple clients outside of organizational contexts, thus removing many central elements of how careers have been conceptualized. Even more fundamentally, jobs, which represent the core building blocks of most careers, are now being threatened by job-deconstruction, referring to the unbundling of formal job roles into discrete job elements like projects or tasks, and matching these with the knowledge, skills, and abilities of employees in the internal labor market. This shift is significant, as the role of jobs has been critical in determining the level of variety, complexity, identity, and meaningfulness experienced in work and in career experiences, and is central to career theories. A shift in focus from jobs to skills shifts this perspective and raises several questions for careers theory.

The temporality of careers is also in flux. While much has been written about the future of work, there is little doubt that the pace of change in skills demands and work design currently being experienced is unprecedented. Recent calls in the management literature for researching forward, prospective, and prescriptive theorizing seem apt for our theorizing of careers as well. While most definitions of career refer to an evolving sequence of experiences over time, most of our theorizing does not fully engage with the temporal dimension of careers. To illustrate, people make sense of their present careers only in the context of their past experiences and in light of their anticipated future, and inevitably, one's present becomes one's past, just as the future takes center stage as the present. As the intensity and speed of change increase and the life cycle of many skills shortens, it is critical to find novel ways to integrate temporality into career theory.

Another undeniable trend impacting careers is the unprecedented impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on work and the workforce. Although the precise impacts are uncertain, early evidence suggests a particular effect on early-career workers. This potentially changes traditional entry routes into organizations and how early-career professionals develop the domain knowledge critical to building their careers. For some, it may compress the timeframe for the expectation to develop from novice to expert in their careers. AI, and particularly agentic AI, may impact the opportunities workers have to build careers in jobs where AI automates rather than augments work, particularly those at risk, and where expert versus non-expert elements of the job are automated. Thus, the impacts of AI on careers are significant and require significant consideration of career theories.

These contemporary trends are a key motivation for emerging career research. The assumptions and boundary conditions of traditional careers theory largely fall short in accounting for the complexity of the contemporary context within which careers unfold. Thus, our understanding of careers today may be limited by theory that fails to account for the more dynamic, relational, and contextually embedded understandings of career development.

This special issue aims to advance scholarly understanding of contemporary careers through novel conceptual perspectives that challenge existing assumptions in careers theory, introduce new theories and frameworks, and shape the research agenda in the field. The special issue focuses on two central questions: (1) How should existing theories and concepts be updated or adjusted to understand and analyze contemporary careers? (2) How can we understand and analyze contemporary careers through new theoretical and conceptual frameworks (newly developed or brought in from other disciplines)? Contributions may develop new theoretical frameworks, synthesize research streams, or critically examine how social, organizational, institutional, and technological forces shape careers. We seek scholarship that integrates insights from a variety of disciplines, including, for example, careers, OB, HRM, and beyond, to rethink foundational assumptions about contemporary careers. In doing so, this special issue aims to shape a new research agenda that addresses fundamental emerging changes in careers.

Potential topics

  • How do ongoing social, technological, and geopolitical disruptions challenge existing assumptions embedded in dominant career theories?
  • How can new conceptual models better account for the relational and contextual aspects of career development in uncertain and changing environments?
  • How should we reconceptualize concepts such as career competencies and employability in labor markets characterized by volatility, automation, and shifting skill demands?
  • How can careers be reconceptualized in non-traditional work, including the gig economy, internal job deconstruction, and entrepreneurship?
  • How do new forms of digital, hybrid, or platform-mediated work reshape notions of career identity, career success, and career self-management?
  • What role does AI, including agentic AI, and the potential role of AI agents as co-workers play in how individuals' careers evolve?
  • How can career theories and concepts be adapted or renewed to capture the career experiences of underrepresented and marginalized groups?
  • How do organizational, institutional, and labor market structures shape individuals' capacity to construct meaningful and sustainable career paths during times of disruption?
  • How do global mobility patterns, migration, and geopolitical conflict reshape traditional narratives of career progression and mobility?
  • What new methodological or conceptual tools are needed to theorize non-linear, fragmented, or cyclical career patterns that increasingly deviate from traditional career models?
